newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Timor celebrates calmly after Christmas eve death.
newsitem.headline: Timor celebrates calmly after Christmas eve death.

text.p: East Timorese celebrated Christmas calmly in the former Portuguese colony a day after a soldier was beaten to death near the cathedral in the capital Dili, police and residents said.

Police said 11 people, mostly soldiers or police, were attacked by the crowd in several incidents on Tuesday when tens of thousands gathered at Dili's Komoro airport and the cathedral to welcome home Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo.

However, Dili was reported calm on Christmas Day as the mostly Catholic population of the territory celebrated by attending church services as a high-profile but not unusual police presence watched from street corners.

"There were no problems with the Christmas celebrations as far as we know. All the churches, including the cathedral, were full and between 2,000 and 3,000 people attended mass this morning at the bishop's residence," one Dili parishioner said.

U.S. Congressman Patrick Kennedy, on a two-day visit to East Timor, said the midnight mass at the cathedral given by Belo was "full of joy" as the people welcomed him back from a European trip during which he received his peace prize in Norway.
East Timor police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam told Reuters the situation in Dili was safe and under control on Wednesday.
He confirmed that one East Timorese soldier had been beaten to death by a crowd of Catholic youths outside the city's main cathedral on Tuesday as thousands gathered to celebrate mass with Belo.
The crowd, estimated by some at over 100,000, had flocked from outside Dili to greet Belo, who also met German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Pope John Paul II on his overseas trip.
Muharam said 11 people were still in hospital with wounds received in attacks by the crowd, mostly on soldiers or police in civilian clothes. Two of the injured were members of the public, he said.
Police had not yet detained anyone after the arrests. "But we will," Muharam said.

Residents said the youths attacked the soldier outside the cathedral before a prayer service after he was found with a pistol and walkie-talkie radio. Muharam said the man was joining prayers at which Belo called on Timorese to be united in peace.
They said rumours had been rife in recent days that an assassination attempt would be made on Belo, who last month said attempts on his life had been made in 1989 and 1991.

Kennedy, the nephew of the late U.S. President John Kennedy, said he met with Indonesian government and military leaders while in Dili, including a meeting with Belo for more than an hour on Christmas day, during his fact-finding trip.
Kennedy said Belo had told him the Indonesian government had recruited and trained many infiltrators among young Timorese.

"(They) have infiltrated into the student movement and the community to provoke disturbances and invite recriminations from the government which (it) uses as excuses for their own activities," Kennedy said.
Kennedy also said he would contine to oppose the proposed sale of F-16 aircraft by the United States to Indonesia as well as oppose American-funded training for Jakarta's military.
Meawhile, Muharam said 46 East Timorese were detained on Tuesday after a dispute between villages in the southern Viqueque district.
"It was a fight between villages. Those who were involved were taken by police," Muharam said from Dili.
Other police sources said about 40 people were still being held for questioning.

One East Timor resident said the tension in recent weeks was between pro-independence youths who had threatened to take action against opponents who had cooperated with Indonesian security authorities, once Timor gained independence.

Mostly Moslem Indonesia still maintains a large security force in East Timor more than 21 years after its December 1975 invasion. Jakarta declared the territory its 27th province in July 1976 in a move not yet recognised by the United Nations.
